original_value: The advent of very high resolution (VHR) satellite imagery and the development of Geographic Object-Based Image Analysis (GEOBIA) have led to many new opportunities for fine-scale land cover mapping, especially in urban areas. Image segmentation is an important step in the GEOBIA framework, so great time/effort is often spent to ensure that computer-generated image segments closely match real-world objects of interest. In the remote sensing community, segmentation is frequently performed using the multiresolution segmentation (MRS) algorithm, which is tuned through three user-defined parameters (the scale, shape/color, and compactness/smoothness parameters). The scale parameter (SP) is the most important parameter and governs the average size of generated image segments. Existing automatic methods to determine suitable SPs for segmentation are scene-specific and often computationally intensive, so an approach to estimating appropriate SPs that is generalizable (i.e., not scene-specific) could speed up the GEOBIA workflow considerably. In this study, we attempted to identify generalizable SPs for five common urban land cover types (buildings, vegetation, roads, bare soil, and water) through meta-analysis and nonlinear regression tree (RT) modeling. First, we performed a literature search of recent studies that employed GEOBIA for urban land cover mapping and extracted the MRS parameters used, the image properties (i.e., spatial and radiometric resolutions), and the land cover classes mapped. Using this data extracted from the literature, we constructed RT models for each land cover class to predict suitable SP values based on the: image spatial resolution, image radiometric resolution, shape/color parameter, and compactness/smoothness parameter. Based on a visual and quantitative analysis of results, we found that for all land cover classes except water, relatively accurate SPs could be identified using our RT modeling results. The main advantage of our approach over existing SP selection approaches is that our RT model results are not scene-specific, so they can be used to quickly identify suitable SPs in other VHR images.

result.paraphrase: Very high resolution (VHR) satellite imagery and Geographic Object-Based Image Analysis (GEOBIA) have created many opportunities for detailed land cover mapping, particularly in urban settings. Because image segmentation is a key step in the GEOBIA workflow, substantial time and effort are often devoted to making computer-generated segments closely correspond to real-world objects of interest. In remote sensing, segmentation is commonly carried out with the multiresolution segmentation (MRS) algorithm, which is controlled by three user-defined parameters: scale, shape/color, and compactness/smoothness. Of these, the scale parameter (SP) is the most critical, as it determines the average size of the resulting image segments. Existing automatic techniques for selecting appropriate SPs are often scene-specific and computationally demanding, so a more generalizable, non-scene-specific method could greatly accelerate GEOBIA processing. In this study, we used meta-analysis and nonlinear regression tree (RT) modeling to seek generalizable SPs for five common urban land cover classes: buildings, vegetation, roads, bare soil, and water. We first searched recent literature on GEOBIA-based urban land cover mapping and extracted the MRS settings used, along with image properties such as spatial and radiometric resolution and the mapped land cover classes. Using the literature-derived data, we built RT models for each class to predict suitable SP values from image spatial resolution, image radiometric resolution, shape/color, and compactness/smoothness parameters. Visual and quantitative evaluation showed that, for all classes except water, relatively accurate SPs could be identified from our RT results. Compared with existing SP selection methods, the chief advantage of our approach is that the RT models are not scene-specific, allowing suitable SPs to be identified quickly in other VHR images.
